407.title: Great by hearsay
407.hook: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe: everyone calls You great from hearing, but only one who has seen knows (Asa, ang 9)
407.howItsDone: Suni vaddaa is the second shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; some Sikh teachers draw from it the reading that hearing about the Divine is a beginning, and knowing for oneself is the goal.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, so dar, and your line, the door at dusk. Did you pause on your own threshold and listen? Today, the second shabad of Rehras, and a very honest question about how we know anything. Day four hundred seven.
screen: `SO DAR — THE DOOR AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: A boy from a village far inland grows up hearing about the sea. His uncle has been. The ocean is huge, the uncle says, bigger than all of Punjab, salty, loud, it never stops moving. The boy repeats it to his friends: the sea is huge. He's right. But he doesn't know it. Years later, he steps off a bus on the coast and walks to the edge of the water, and he goes completely quiet. He never says the sea is huge again. Today: great by hearsay.
screen: `A BOY WHO HAS HEARD ABOUT THE SEA.` → `HE REPEATS IT: THE SEA IS HUGE.` → `THEN HE SEES IT, AND GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: The second shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak again, in Raag Asa, begins: suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe. Hearing, everyone calls You great. And then, in paraphrase: but how great You are, only someone who has seen can say. That's a startling way to open an evening prayer. It admits that talk about God can be hearsay: things we were told and repeated, secondhand. Guru Nanak doesn't mock it. Everyone says You're great, and they're right. But hearing is not the same as seeing. Then the shabad does something even more honest. It says those who did see couldn't describe it either. Your worth can't be estimated, it says, and can't be spoken. Those who tried to describe You were absorbed into You. The refrain calls out: my great Master, deep and profound, an ocean of virtue, nobody knows how vast You are. All the meditators met and meditated, it says; all the appraisers met and appraised; the scholars and teachers tried; and none of them could tell even a sliver. So the shabad leaves us between two things. Hearsay isn't enough, and seeing leaves you speechless. Like the boy at the sea. Some readers set this beside the Japji's suniai pauris: hearing as a real beginning, and seeing, knowing for yourself, as where the path goes. For the evening, the question is simple. What, today, did you actually see, not just hear about? Seen, not heard.
screen: `SUNI VADDAA: GREAT, FROM HEARING.` · `ONLY ONE WHO HAS SEEN CAN SAY.` · `THOSE WHO SAW WERE LEFT SPEECHLESS.` · `HEARING BEGINS; SEEING IS THE PATH.` · then, large: `SEEN, NOT HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what you have seen, not heard. Think back over today, or yesterday. Find one thing you saw with your own eyes or felt for yourself: a kindness, a sky, a moment of peace, a moment of fear that passed. Not something you read about. Something you were there for. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence. I saw. I felt. Then sit with it quietly, the way the boy stood at the water. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Great by hearsay. Suni vaddaa aakhai sabh koe: everyone calls the Lord great from hearing; only one who has seen knows, and even they can't describe it.
screen: `GREAT BY HEARSAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seen, not heard. Today, when you're about to pass on something you only heard, notice it, and share something you actually saw instead. Day four hundred seven.

screen: `DAY 407 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: REMEMBERING, I LIVE.`

fork.reveal: Guru Nanak says hearing is not seeing, and then admits that those who saw were left speechless: the Lord's worth can't be told.

408.title: Remembering, I live
408.hook: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: chanting I live, forgetting I die (Asa, ang 9)
408.howItsDone: Aakhaa jeevaa is the third shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; remembering the Name, simran, through the day is central to Sikh practice, and some Sikhs repeat Waheguru quietly while they work.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, great by hearsay, and your line, seen, not heard. Did you share something you actually saw? Today, the third shabad of Rehras, and it's about forgetting. Day four hundred eight.
screen: `GREAT BY HEARSAY — SEEN, NOT HEARD.`

segments.voice: A busy day. Meetings back to back, errands, messages. Somewhere around noon you meant to eat and didn't. By four o'clock you're snapping at people, the screen is blurry, everything feels harder than it should. And then it hits you: I forgot lunch. You weren't failing at life. You'd just forgotten the thing that keeps you going, and the cost showed up everywhere else. Tonight's shabad reaches for hunger too. Today: remembering, I live.
screen: `A BUSY DAY. LUNCH FORGOTTEN.` → `BY FOUR, EVERYTHING IS HARDER.` → `OH. I FORGOT TO EAT.`

segments.voice: The third shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with this line: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao. Saying it, I live; forgetting, I die. It, here, is the Name. Then, straight away, honesty: it's hard to say the True Name. Not hard to pronounce. Hard to keep saying, to keep remembering, through a day full of everything else. And then the hunger picture. If a person feels hunger for the True Name, the shabad says in paraphrase, that hunger eats up their pain. That's a reversal. Usually hunger is the problem. Here, the right hunger is the cure: wanting the Name so much that the wanting itself consumes sorrow. The refrain asks: so kio visrai meree maae. How could I forget Him, my mother? You've heard that address before: meree maae, my mother, is how the Anand began. Here it's a plea, almost a worry: how could I ever forget? The shabad goes on to say that even if everyone gathered to praise Him, He wouldn't grow greater, and if no one did, He wouldn't grow less. He doesn't die, and there's no mourning for Him; He keeps on giving, and His gifts never run out. So remembering isn't for His sake. It's for ours. The remembering is the lunch. Forget it, and by four o'clock the whole soul is running on empty. Remember, and live.
screen: `AAKHAA JEEVAA: SAYING IT, I LIVE.` · `IT'S HARD TO KEEP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HUNGER FOR THE NAME EATS PAIN.` · `HOW COULD I FORGET, MY MOTHER?` · then, large: `REMEMBER AND LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember once at dusk. Sit and let the day's noise settle a little. Then, gently, remember. If you pray, remember the Name: say Waheguru once, slowly, and let it be the meal you skipped. If you don't, remember the one thing that keeps you going: a person, a purpose, a quiet you trust. Hold it for a few breaths. When the mind wanders back into the day, that's forgetting. Notice it, and remember again. That's the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Remembering. Aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: saying the Name, I live; forgetting it, I die. The third shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak.
screen: `REMEMBERING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: remember and live. Today, set one small reminder, a note on the fridge, an alarm at dusk, and when it goes off, remember once. Day four hundred eight.

screen: `DAY 408 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SO PURAKH: THAT BEING.`

options: it makes life harder.
hunger for the Name eats up pain.
it should be cured by fasting.
fork.reveal: usually hunger is the problem; here, hunger for the True Name is the cure, consuming sorrow.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aakhaa jeevaa, saying it, I live; the opening of the third shabad of Rehras.

trapdoor: what you thought: remembering, I live is a poetic exaggeration.
what it means: remembering the Name is like the meal that keeps you going; forget it and the soul runs on empty.
what a scholar hears: the shabad pairs aakhan (saying) with visarna (forgetting), and its refrain, so kio visrai meree maae, puts the fear of forgetting as a question to 'my mother'.

sources.ref: Asa M1, aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao, Ang 9

409.title: So Purakh: that Being
409.hook: so purakh niranjan: that Being is pure, beyond reach, and all meditate on Him (Asa M4, ang 10–11)
409.howItsDone: So Purakh is the first of four shabads in the second group of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; in kirtan it can be sung slowly, its doubled phrases repeated.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering, and your line, remember and live. Did your reminder go off, and did you remember once? Today, a second group of shabads inside Rehras, and a new voice. Day four hundred nine.
screen: `REMEMBERING — REMEMBER AND LIVE.`

segments.voice: Kajal, the black eyeliner, can be made at home by an old method. You light a small oil lamp and hold a clay or brass plate just above the flame. In a few minutes the underside is coated in soft black soot. Scrape it off, mix it with a little ghee, and you have kajal. The flame itself stays bright and clean. Everything it touches turns black. That old word for soot and eyeliner, anjan, is hiding inside today's line. Today: So Purakh, that Being.
screen: `A PLATE HELD OVER A LAMP.` → `SOOT: THE OLD WAY TO MAKE KAJAL.` → `THE FLAME STAYS CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Rehras has two more shabads in its first group, and we'll come back to them in a few days. Today we jump to the second group, called So Purakh after its opening words. The voice changes too. These are by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru. It opens: so purakh niranjan. That Being, purakh, is niranjan. Nir means without. Anjan is that soot, the black of kajal, and so a stain. Niranjan: without a stain. Untouched by the soot of the world, the way the flame stays clean while the plate turns black. The line goes on: the Lord, beyond reach, beyond reach, without limit. Then, in paraphrase: all meditate on You, all meditate on You, true Creator. All beings are Yours, and You are the giver to every being. Meditate on the Lord, saints; He takes away every sorrow. And then a line that turns everything inward: the Lord Himself is the master, and the Lord Himself is the servant. What is poor Nanak? Guru Ram Das signs with the name Nanak, as the Gurus whose hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib do. Notice the repeating. Beyond reach, beyond reach. All meditate, all meditate. The words circle, the way a lamp flame flickers but stays a flame. In kirtan, So Purakh can be sung slowly, the lines doubling back. The picture it leaves at dusk is simple: whatever soot the day has left on you, that Being is untouched by it. Pure being.
screen: `SO PURAKH: GURU RAM DAS'S SHABADS.` · `NIRANJAN: WITHOUT A STAIN, NO SOOT.` · `ALL MEDITATE ON YOU, GIVER OF ALL.` · `HIMSELF THE MASTER, HIMSELF THE SERVANT.` · then, large: `PURE BEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say so purakh niranjan. Slowly, three times, out loud or under your breath. So purakh niranjan. So purakh niranjan. So purakh niranjan. Then let the words go and picture a lamp flame: steady, bright, clean, while everything around it gathers soot. Let the day's smudges be on the plate, not the flame. Breathe with that picture for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once at the end. The bell holds the time.
So Purakh. That Being: the opening of Guru Ram Das's shabads in Rehras. So purakh niranjan: that Being is without stain, beyond reach, the giver of all.
screen: `SO PURAKH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pure being. Tonight, if you see a candle or a lamp, or even a stove flame, look at it for one breath and remember niranjan. Day four hundred nine.

screen: `DAY 409 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU ARE THE TRUE CREATOR.`

fork.setup: Guru Ram Das calls that Being niranjan. what picture is inside the word?
options: a mountain no one can climb.

a door that's always open.
fork.reveal: anjan is soot, the black of kajal; niranjan is without it, untouched by the world's stain.

original.note: Gurmukhi: niranjan, without stain; from nir, without, and anjan, soot or kajal.

trapdoor: what you thought: so purakh niranjan is a string of holy names.
what it means: that Being is without stain, beyond reach, the giver of all, and Himself both master and servant.
what a scholar hears: niranjan is an old Indic term, nir plus anjan, collyrium or soot; it was used in Nath and Sant traditions too, and gurbani uses it for the One beyond maya.

sources.ref: Asa M4, so purakh niranjan, Ang 10–11

410.title: You are the true Creator
410.hook: too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee: You are the true Creator, my Master (Asa M4, ang 11)
410.tomorrow: A pool of fire and water
410.howItsDone: Too kartaa sachiaar is the second shabad of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its line that the Lord is the river within which all things are is often quoted in Sikh teaching.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, So Purakh, and your line, pure being. Did you see a flame and remember niranjan? Today, Guru Ram Das's second shabad, and it speaks straight to the Maker. Day four hundred ten.
screen: `SO PURAKH — PURE BEING.`

segments.voice: Pick up a handmade bowl at a craft fair and turn it over. On the bottom, pressed into the clay, there's often a little mark: initials, a symbol, the potter's stamp. The bowl doesn't know it's there. It just holds soup. But the mark says someone shaped this, on purpose, with their hands. Guru Ram Das looks at a whole day that way: the light this morning, the people in it, the breath you're breathing now. Tonight's shabad turns the day over and reads the mark. Today: You are the true Creator.
screen: `A HANDMADE BOWL, TURNED OVER.` → `THE POTTER'S MARK ON THE BASE.` → `TONIGHT: READ THE MARK ON THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The second So Purakh shabad, by Guru Ram Das, opens: too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee. You are the true Creator, my Master. Kartaa is the maker, the same word as in the Mool Mantar's karta purakh. Sachiaar is true. And maiddaa saanee, my Master, is said in western Punjabi forms, the speech of the plains around Multan, so even the grammar sounds like someone talking at home. Then, in paraphrase: whatever pleases You comes to pass; whatever You give, that is what I receive. All belongs to You, and all meditate on You. The one You bless receives the jewel of the Name. The shabad gives the two directions a person can face: the gurmukh, turned toward the Guru, finds it; the manmukh, turned toward the self, loses it. Then come two pictures. You Yourself separate us, the shabad says, and You Yourself bring us together. And: You are the river, and everything is within You; without You, there is no other. All beings are Your play. So the Maker isn't standing outside the day, like a potter who walked away from the wheel. The Maker is the river the whole day flows in. For Sikhs saying Rehras, that changes what thank you means at dusk: not thanks sent off to a distant address, but the bowl noticing the hands still holding it. And the closing note is trust, said simply: You are my Master.
screen: `TOO KARTAA SACHIAAR: YOU ARE THE TRUE MAKER.` · `WHAT YOU GIVE IS WHAT I RECEIVE.` · `GURMUKH FINDS, MANMUKH LOSES.` · `YOU ARE THE RIVER; ALL IS IN YOU.` · then, large: `MY MASTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the maker of your day. Turn today over, like the bowl, and look underneath. Find three things you didn't make yourself: the morning light, someone who cooked or drove or helped, the breath itself. Let each one come to mind slowly. For each, a quiet thank you. If you pray, you can say the shabad's own words, too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee, or simply Waheguru. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
You are the true Creator. Too kartaa sachiaar maiddaa saanee: Guru Ram Das calls the Lord the true Maker and his Master, the river in which everything flows.
screen: `YOU ARE THE TRUE CREATOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: my master. Today, when something arrives that you didn't plan, good or hard, try saying inside: what You give, I receive. Day four hundred ten.

screen: `DAY 410 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A POOL OF FIRE AND WATER.`

411.title: A pool of fire and water
411.word: A pool of fire and water
411.hook: in the world's pool we dwell, where water and fire both are, feet stuck in the mud of attachment (Asa M1, ang 12)
411.tomorrow: This human body is your chance
411.howItsDone: This shabad is the third of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; Sikh teachers cite its closing line when explaining the place of sangat, the company of those who remember, in Sikh life.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, You are the true Creator, and your line, my master. Did something unplanned arrive, and could you receive it? Tonight's shabad is darker, and very honest. Day four hundred eleven.
screen: `YOU ARE THE TRUE CREATOR — MY MASTER.`

segments.voice: Monsoon in a Punjabi village. The field path has turned to thick brown mud. You step off the bricks, and your foot sinks to the ankle. You pull. The mud pulls back. You pull harder, and your foot comes out, without the shoe. Mud like that has a rule: the harder you yank, the tighter it holds. Guru Nanak pictures the world as a pool with mud like that. Today: a pool of fire and water.
screen: `MONSOON. A FIELD PATH TURNED TO MUD.` → `THE HARDER YOU PULL, THE TIGHTER IT HOLDS.` → `GURU NANAK SAW THE WORLD LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: The third So Purakh shabad is by Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa. It begins, in paraphrase: we live in that pool, and He made both water and fire there. A pool where water and fire live together: things that cool and things that burn, comfort and craving, side by side. Then the mud. In the mud of attachment, moh, the feet can't move. I have seen people drowning there. Moh is the clinging kind of love: to things, to status, to having it our way. It doesn't feel like a trap. It feels like the ground. Then the shabad turns to the mind: foolish mind, you don't remember the One. Forgetting the Lord, your virtues waste away. And then a turn. Guru Nanak doesn't present himself as the one standing safely on the bank. He says, in effect: I'm not a celibate ascetic, I'm not a model of virtue, I'm not learned. My life has been foolish and ignorant. Then the closing line: Nanak prays, I seek the shelter of those who have not forgotten You. So the way out of the mud isn't pulling harder on your own. It's reaching for a hand: the company of people who remember, the sangat. Not willpower alone, and not leaving the world behind. The shabad stays in the pool of fire and water, and reaches for those who remember. Out of the mud.
screen: `A POOL WHERE WATER AND FIRE LIVE.` · `MOH: THE MUD THAT HOLDS THE FEET.` · `NOT CELIBATE, NOT VIRTUOUS, NOT LEARNED.` · `SHELTER WITH THOSE WHO REMEMBER.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift your feet and wiggle your toes. If you're sitting, raise both feet a little off the floor and wiggle your toes. Feel how free they are right now. Set them down. Then think of one thing that's been holding your feet lately: a grudge, a habit, a worry you keep feeding. Don't yank at it. Just name it. Then think of one person who remembers, someone steady, and picture taking their hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
A pool of fire and water. Guru Nanak's picture of the world in Rehras: water and fire together, feet stuck in the mud of attachment, and shelter with those who haven't forgotten the Lord.
screen: `A POOL OF FIRE AND WATER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: out of the mud. Today, when you feel stuck, instead of pulling harder alone, reach out to one steady person, even with a short message. Day four hundred eleven.

screen: `DAY 411 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THIS HUMAN BODY IS YOUR CHANCE.`

412.title: This human body is your chance
412.word: This human body is your chance
412.hook: bhaee paraapat maanukh dehureeaa: you have this human body; now is your chance (Asa M5, ang 12)
412.howItsDone: Bhaee paraapat is the last shabad of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its opening line is quoted in Sikh teaching about the preciousness of human life.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pool of fire and water, and your line, out of the mud. Did you reach for one steady person? Tonight, the last So Purakh shabad, and it's about time. Day four hundred twelve.
screen: `A POOL OF FIRE AND WATER — OUT OF THE MUD.`

segments.voice: A crowded government office. You took a paper ticket an hour ago: number 147. The screen says 139. You scroll your phone, check the time, scroll again. 143. You go to get water. 145. You answer a message from your cousin. And then you look up and the screen says 149, and a voice is calling a number that isn't yours anymore. Your turn came, and passed, while you were looking somewhere else. Guru Arjan uses that very idea, a turn. Today: this human body is your chance.
screen: `TICKET 147. THE SCREEN SAYS 139.` → `SCROLLING, WATER, A MESSAGE.` → `THE SCREEN SAYS 149.`

segments.voice: The fourth So Purakh shabad is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. It opens: bhaee paraapat maanukh dehureeaa. You have received this human body. Then: gobind milan kee eh teree bareeaa. This is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe. Bareeaa is a turn, like a turn in a queue, or your turn at the well. Sikh teaching speaks of the soul passing through many lives, and of a human birth as rare and precious, the one in which a person can consciously remember the One. So the shabad says, in paraphrase: other work won't help you here. Join the company of the holy and meditate on the Name alone. Put your effort into crossing the frightening ocean of the world; your life is slipping away in the color of maya. Notice it doesn't say other work is evil. Sikhs work, raise families and run businesses; Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan building the Harmandir Sahib. It says other work can't do this particular job. Then, like Guru Nanak yesterday, Guru Arjan turns humble. I haven't practiced meditation, austerity, self-control or right living, he says. I haven't served the holy or known the Lord. Nanak says: my deeds are lowly. I have come to Your shelter; protect my honor. So the chance isn't something to earn by being impressive. It's a turn that's already come. The number on the screen is yours, right now. Now is the chance.
screen: `MAANUKH DEHUREEAA: THIS HUMAN BODY.` · `BAREEAA: YOUR TURN TO MEET THE LORD.` · `OTHER WORK CAN'T DO THIS ONE JOB.` · `MY DEEDS ARE LOWLY; I SEEK YOUR SHELTER.` · then, large: `NOW IS THE CHANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do today's good now. Think of one good thing you've been meaning to do: a call to someone lonely, an apology, a donation, a thank-you note. Something small enough to start today. Picture yourself doing it. Then decide when, exactly, today, you'll begin, and if you can, take the first tiny step as soon as the bell ends. For now, rest with the breath, and with the line: this is your turn. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
This human body is your chance. Bhaee paraapat maanukh dehureeaa: Guru Arjan says this human life is your turn to meet the Lord, so don't let it pass.

413.title: The humble plea
413.hook: the Lord's humble servants ask the True Guru for the Name (Gujri M4, ang 10)
413.howItsDone: Har ke jan satgur satpurkhaa is the fourth shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its line naming the Lord's praise as rahraas is often given as the source of the prayer's name.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, this human body is your chance, and your line, now is the chance. Did you take the first small step on something good? Today we step back to a shabad we skipped, and it holds the name of the whole prayer. Day four hundred thirteen.
screen: `YOUR CHANCE — NOW IS THE CHANCE.`

segments.voice: Some people find it easy to ask for help. Others would rather drive around lost for an hour than ask for directions. They say I'm fine, I've got it, don't worry about me, and then carry it alone. Asking can feel like admitting you're small. Guru Ram Das, a Guru the sangat bowed to, wrote a shabad that is nothing but asking, and calls himself very small indeed. Today: the humble plea.
screen: `DRIVING LOST RATHER THAN ASKING.` → `I'M FINE, I'VE GOT IT.` → `A GURU'S SHABAD THAT ONLY ASKS.`

segments.voice: In Rehras, after the three shabads we heard a few days ago, come two more in Raag Gujri, before the So Purakh group. We're going back for them now. The first is by Guru Ram Das. It begins, in paraphrase: O servant of the Lord, True Guru, True Being, I make my plea to the Guru. We are worms and insects, True Guru, and we seek Your shelter. Be kind, and let the light of the Name shine. Worms and insects. Guru Ram Das was the fourth Guru, remembered in Sikh tradition as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. And here he speaks as the smallest of creatures, asking. Then the refrain: my friend, divine Guru, light up the Lord's Name in me. And then a line you'll recognize. Through the Guru's teaching, the Name is the friend of my breath, and the Lord's praise is my rahraas. Rahraas. The very word the evening prayer is named for, provisions for the road. Here it's in the text: my provisions are the praise of the Lord. The shabad goes on: great is the fortune of the Lord's servants who have faith in Him and thirst for Him. So this is what a plea looks like in Sikh prayer. Not bargaining, not a list of demands. An honest admission of smallness, and a request for the one thing that matters: the Name. The word for it here is binau, a humble petition. It's the same spirit as Ardas, where Sikhs stand and ask, with folded hands. The humble ask.
screen: `TWO GUJRI SHABADS, BEFORE SO PURAKH.` · `WE ARE WORMS AND INSECTS; WE SEEK SHELTER.` · `THE LORD'S PRAISE IS MY RAHRAAS.` · `BINAU: A HUMBLE PETITION FOR THE NAME.` · then, large: `THE HUMBLE ASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help once. Think of something you've been carrying alone. Then think of who could help: a friend, a sibling, a colleague, a doctor. If you pray, you might bring it to God first, in the plain words of your own heart, or say Waheguru once. Then, sometime today, ask a person. Keep it small and honest: could you help me with this? For now, just picture asking, and notice what it feels like in your chest. Breathe through it. The bell holds the time.
The humble plea. Guru Ram Das asks the True Guru for the light of the Name. This week: hearsay, remembering, that Being, the true Creator, the muddy pool, your chance, and now the humble ask.
screen: `THE HUMBLE PLEA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the humble ask. Today, ask one person for help with one real thing, plainly, without apologizing for asking. Day four hundred thirteen.

screen: `DAY 413 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WORRY, MIND.`
